text: The lysine side chain carries a positively charged (protonated) epsilon-amino group at physiological pH because its side-chain pKa is about 10.5, well above 7.4.
The aspartate and glutamate side chains are negatively charged at physiological pH because their carboxyl side chains (pKa around 3.7-4.2) are deprotonated well below pH 7.4.

Histidine is the only standard amino acid whose side-chain pKa (about 6) is near physiological pH, so its imidazole group can shift between protonated and neutral around pH 7 and act as a biological buffer.
The isoelectric point (pI) of an amino acid or protein is the pH at which its net charge is zero, so at that pH it does not migrate in an electric field.
For a simple amino acid with no ionizable side chain, the pI is estimated as the average of the alpha-carboxyl and alpha-amino pKa values.
Below its pI a protein carries a net positive charge and above its pI it carries a net negative charge, because lowering pH protonates ionizable groups and raising pH deprotonates them.
The Michaelis constant Km is the substrate concentration at which an enzyme's reaction rate is half of Vmax, and a lower Km reflects higher apparent affinity of the enzyme for its substrate.
When substrate concentration is far above Km the enzyme is saturated, so the reaction rate approaches Vmax and becomes nearly independent of further increases in substrate.
When substrate concentration is far below Km the reaction rate is approximately proportional to substrate concentration, so the reaction is roughly first-order in substrate in that regime.
A competitive inhibitor raises an enzyme's apparent Km while leaving Vmax unchanged, because it competes with substrate for the active site and can be outcompeted at high substrate concentration.
A noncompetitive inhibitor lowers an enzyme's Vmax while leaving Km unchanged, because it binds a site other than the active site and cannot be overcome by adding more substrate.
On a Lineweaver-Burk double-reciprocal plot the y-intercept equals 1/Vmax and the x-intercept equals -1/Km, so a change in either intercept reveals which kinetic parameter an inhibitor has altered.
Many enzymes require a cofactor, such as a metal ion or an organic coenzyme, to be catalytically active; the inactive protein alone is the apoenzyme and the complete active form is the holoenzyme.
Ohm's law states that the voltage across an ohmic resistor equals the current through it times its resistance (V = IR), so resistance can be found as R = V/I.
An ohmic conductor shows a current that increases linearly with the applied voltage at constant temperature, which is the defining behavior that distinguishes ohmic from non-ohmic components.
Resistors in series add directly, so the equivalent resistance of a series combination is the sum of the individual resistances and is always larger than any one of them.

For resistors in parallel the reciprocals of the resistances add, so the equivalent resistance is smaller than the smallest individual resistor; two equal resistors in parallel give half of one resistor's value.
The power dissipated by a resistor equals current times voltage (P = IV), which combined with Ohm's law also equals I squared times R or V squared divided by R.
Kirchhoff's current law states that the total current entering a junction equals the total current leaving it, a direct consequence of conservation of charge.
In a series circuit the same current flows through every element, while in a parallel circuit the same voltage appears across each branch.
Operant conditioning is learning in which the consequences of a voluntary behavior change how often that behavior occurs, as described by B. F. Skinner.
Reinforcement increases a behavior: positive reinforcement adds a desirable stimulus after the behavior, while negative reinforcement removes an aversive stimulus after the behavior.
Punishment decreases a behavior: positive punishment adds an aversive stimulus after the behavior, while negative punishment removes a desirable stimulus after the behavior.
A variable-ratio reinforcement schedule delivers reinforcement after an unpredictable number of responses and produces a high, steady rate of responding that is highly resistant to extinction.

A fixed-interval schedule reinforces the first response after a set amount of time has passed, producing a scalloped response pattern in which responding slows just after reinforcement and speeds up as the next interval ends.
Shaping is an operant technique that reinforces successive approximations of a target behavior, gradually guiding an organism toward a complex response it would rarely perform spontaneously.
